q: Which list contains only essential elements of a valid contract?
options: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, legal purpose
Competent parties, notarization, recording, legal purpose
Offer, earnest money, title insurance, consideration
Written form, recording, consideration, broker signature
wrong: Notarization and recording are not required for a contract to be valid.
Earnest money and title insurance are common but not essential elements.
Recording and a broker's signature are not essential elements.
why: Every valid contract needs competent parties, mutual assent through offer and acceptance, consideration, and a legal purpose.
hook: COAL: Competent, Offer and acceptance, consideration, Legal.

q: Under the statute of frauds, a contract for the sale of real estate must be:
options: In writing and signed by the party to be charged
Approved by the Real Estate Division
wrong: Recording gives public notice but isn't what makes the contract enforceable.
Notarization is needed to record a deed, not to make a sale contract enforceable.
The Division does not approve individual sale contracts.
why: The statute of frauds makes contracts to sell land enforceable only if they are written and signed.
hook: Land deals live on paper.

q: A 17-year-old signs a contract to buy a condo. The contract is:
wrong: A minor's contract isn't void. It stands unless the minor chooses to cancel.
Only the minor, the protected party, has the right to cancel.
The minor can disaffirm the contract.
why: Contracts with minors are voidable at the minor's option. The adult party is still bound.
hook: Voidable is the protected party's choice.

q: A contract to lease a building for an illegal gambling operation is:
wrong: Voidable contracts are valid until someone cancels; an illegal purpose means there was never a contract.
A contract with an illegal purpose isn't valid at all.
Signatures can't make an illegal purpose legal.
why: A contract with an illegal purpose is void. It has no legal effect from the start.
hook: Void is nothing.

q: Two neighbors agree out loud on a price for a vacant lot and shake hands. The agreement is best described as:
wrong: It isn't void; the elements may exist, but a court won't enforce it without a writing.
Voidable means one protected party may cancel; that isn't the problem here.
Executed means fully performed; nothing has been performed.
why: An oral contract to sell land may be valid between the parties, but under the statute of frauds a court won't enforce it.
hook: Land deals live on paper.

q: A purchase agreement in which the buyer promises to pay and the seller promises to convey is a:
wrong: In a unilateral contract only one party promises.
The terms are stated in words, so it's express, not implied.
Nothing here makes it void.
why: When both parties exchange promises, the contract is bilateral.
hook: Bi means both promise.

q: A signed purchase agreement that hasn't closed yet is:
wrong: Executed means fully performed, which happens at closing.
A signed agreement meeting all elements isn't void.
Both parties made promises, so it's bilateral.
why: A contract that still has obligations to be performed is executory.
hook: Executory: the work is still in the story.

q: A broker starts showing a buyer homes, the buyer accepts the help, and both act as if the broker represents the buyer, though nothing was said or written. This may create a(n):
wrong: An express contract is stated in words.
An option gives a right to buy on set terms; that isn't happening here.
Novation replaces an existing contract.
why: Conduct alone can create an implied contract, including an implied agency.
hook: Actions can sign a contract too.

q: A buyer calls you and says, "Tell the seller I'll pay $380,000. We don't need paperwork." What should the agent do?
options: Explain that an offer to buy real estate must be in writing and prepare a written offer for the buyer to sign
Call the seller and accept on the buyer's behalf
Tell the seller the buyer has made a binding offer
Wait to see if the seller calls back
wrong: The agent can't accept anything for the buyer, and there's no seller acceptance to give.
An oral offer to buy land isn't enforceable, so calling it binding misleads the seller.
Doing nothing fails the buyer.
why: Real estate contracts must be in writing to be enforceable. Put the offer in writing and have the buyer sign it.
hook: Land deals live on paper.

q: A seller signs a contract only because the buyer threatened them. The contract is:
wrong: Duress makes a contract voidable, not void.
A party forced to sign can cancel.
The buyer caused the duress and has no right to cancel.
why: Duress, menace, fraud, and undue influence make a contract voidable by the injured party.
hook: Forced to sign? Free to cancel.

q: Consideration in a contract must always be money.
wrong: Consideration can be anything of legal value, including a promise or an act.
why: False. A promise, an act, or property can be consideration.
hook: A promise can pay for a promise.

q: In a unilateral contract, only one party makes a promise.
wrong: That's exactly what makes it unilateral: a promise in exchange for an act.
why: True. The other party can accept only by performing the requested act.
hook: Uni means one promises.

q: A purchase agreement must be recorded with the county to be valid.
wrong: Recording gives public notice. It isn't required for the contract to be valid between the parties.
why: False. Recording isn't an element of a valid contract.
hook: Recording warns the world. It doesn't make the deal.

q: "Meeting of the minds" refers to which contract element?
wrong: Consideration is what each party gives.
Legal purpose concerns what the contract is for.
Competency concerns who can contract.
why: Mutual assent, shown by offer and acceptance, is the meeting of the minds.
hook: Minds meet when an offer is accepted.

q: After closing, a buyer says the seller orally promised to leave the hot tub, but the signed contract lists the included items and doesn't mention it. Under the parol evidence rule, generally:
options: The written contract controls over earlier oral statements
The oral promise controls because it came first
The buyer automatically gets the hot tub
wrong: The rule works the opposite way: the final writing wins.
Courts generally won't let earlier oral terms contradict a complete written contract.
Without a written term, the buyer has no automatic right to it.
why: The parol evidence rule generally bars earlier or same-time oral statements from changing a complete written contract.
hook: Get it in the paper, or it isn't in the deal.

q: A contract that both parties have fully performed is:
wrong: Executory means performance is still due.
Voidable concerns a right to cancel, not performance.
Bilateral describes the promises, not whether they're performed.
why: An executed contract has been completely performed.
hook: Executed: done and dusted.

q: A buyer assigns their purchase contract to a friend. Unless released, the original buyer:
options: Remains liable if the friend fails to perform
Must record the assignment to be released
wrong: Automatic release happens with novation, not assignment.
Assignment creates no agency relationship.
Recording doesn't release anyone.
why: In an assignment the assignor usually stays secondarily liable unless the other party agrees to a release.
hook: Assign and you still sign for it.

q: Substituting a new party for an original party and releasing the original party is called:
wrong: Assignment doesn't release the original party.
Rescission cancels the contract altogether.
Subordination changes lien priority.
why: Novation replaces a party or contract and releases the old one.
hook: Novation sets you free.

q: A seller refuses to close because a higher offer came in. Which remedy best fits a buyer who wants the property itself?
wrong: Liquidated damages pay money, not the property.
Rescission undoes the contract, the opposite of what the buyer wants.
Novation substitutes a party; it isn't a breach remedy.
why: Because land is unique, a court may order the seller to perform and convey the property.
hook: Land is unique, so courts can make you sell.

q: A purchase agreement says that if the buyer defaults, the seller keeps the earnest money as full damages. This is a:
wrong: Specific performance would force the buyer to buy, not set money damages.
A contingency is a condition, not a damages agreement.
Novation substitutes a contract or party.
why: An amount agreed in advance as damages for breach is liquidated damages.
hook: Liquidated: damages settled ahead of time.

q: Buyer and seller both agree to cancel their contract and return the deposit. This is:
wrong: No one failed to perform; they agreed to end it.
Specific performance enforces a contract.
Assignment transfers rights to someone else.
why: Both parties agreeing to cancel and restore each other to their original positions is mutual rescission.
hook: Rescind: rewind the deal.

q: A contract says "time is of the essence" and requires closing by May 15. The buyer is ready on May 18. Most likely:
options: The buyer is in breach for missing the deadline
The contract converts to an option
wrong: With time of the essence, deadlines are strict.
Missing a deadline doesn't create an option.
Nothing extends the deadline automatically.
why: A "time is of the essence" clause makes deadlines strictly enforceable, so missing one is a breach.
hook: When time is of the essence, late is broken.

q: The law that limits how long a party has to file a lawsuit for breach of contract is the:
wrong: The statute of frauds requires certain contracts to be in writing.
The parol evidence rule limits oral evidence about written contracts.
Laches is a related idea about unreasonable delay, but the time limit set by law is the statute of limitations.
why: Each state sets time limits for filing suits; that's the statute of limitations.
hook: Limitations: the clock on lawsuits.

q: Money awarded to cover the actual loss caused by a breach is called:
wrong: Liquidated damages are set in advance in the contract.
Specific performance orders performance, not money.
Consideration is what parties exchange to form a contract.
why: Compensatory damages make the injured party whole for actual losses.
hook: Compensate the loss.

q: Before closing, a wildfire destroys the home and the contract says the risk of loss stays with the seller. The buyer may most likely:
options: Cancel the contract and get the earnest money back
Be forced to close at full price
Sue the listing broker for the loss
wrong: The contract puts the risk on the seller, so the buyer isn't forced to buy a destroyed home.
The broker didn't cause the fire.
There's no basis to hold it open indefinitely.
why: When the seller bears the risk of loss and the property is destroyed, the buyer can generally cancel and recover the deposit.
hook: Read who carries the risk before the fire.

q: Your seller asks whether they can sue the buyer who walked away two days before closing. What should the agent do?
options: Explain the contract terms they can see, and recommend the seller talk to a real estate attorney about legal remedies
Tell the seller exactly how much they will win in court
Draft a lawsuit for the seller
Tell the seller nothing can be done
wrong: Predicting legal outcomes is legal advice the agent isn't licensed to give.
Drafting legal pleadings is the practice of law.
That's false and could cost the seller rights they have.
why: Agents can point to contract terms but must refer legal questions about remedies to an attorney.
hook: Point to the paper, refer the law.

q: Most real estate contracts can be assigned unless the contract prohibits assignment.
wrong: Contracts are generally assignable unless they say otherwise or involve personal services.
why: True. Assignment is allowed unless the contract forbids it or it's a personal service contract.
hook: Assignable unless it says no.

q: Personal service contracts, such as a listing agreement, can generally be assigned to any broker without the owner's consent.
wrong: The owner hired a specific broker, so personal service contracts generally can't be assigned without consent.
why: False. Personal service contracts generally can't be assigned without consent.
hook: You hired a person, not a placeholder.

q: Rescission returns the parties to their positions before the contract was made.
wrong: That's the purpose of rescission.
why: True. Rescission unwinds the contract.
hook: Rescind: rewind the deal.

q: A buyer put down 3% earnest money on a $420,000 purchase. The contract makes the earnest money the seller's liquidated damages. The buyer defaults. How much does the seller keep?
formula: Earnest money = price × earnest money percent
why: The seller keeps the agreed liquidated damages: 3% of $420,000, which is $12,600.
hook: Liquidated: damages settled ahead of time.

q: Failing, without a legal excuse, to do what a contract requires is:
wrong: Rescission is canceling by agreement or right.
Novation substitutes a new contract or party.
Assignment transfers rights.
why: Nonperformance without a legal excuse is a breach of contract.
hook: No excuse, no performance: breach.

q: A seller agreed to repaint the house before closing but used a slightly different shade of white. A court is most likely to treat this as:
options: Substantial performance, possibly with a small damages adjustment
A total breach that cancels the sale
wrong: A trivial deviation usually isn't enough to cancel the whole contract.
Nothing suggests intent to deceive.
No new contract or party was substituted.
why: When performance is essentially complete with a minor deviation, courts often find substantial performance.
hook: Close enough counts, minus the difference.

q: Under an exclusive right to sell listing, the owner finds a buyer with no help from the broker. The broker is:
wrong: That's the exclusive agency rule, not exclusive right to sell.
Nothing in this listing type splits the commission when the owner sells.
The broker is owed the full agreed commission, not just expenses.
why: In an exclusive right to sell, the broker is paid no matter who sells.
hook: Right to sell means the right to be paid.

q: Under an exclusive agency listing, the owner sells the home to a coworker without any broker. The broker is:
options: Owed a referral fee by law
Owed commission only if the sale closes
wrong: The owner kept the right to sell without paying.
No law requires a referral fee here.
Closing doesn't matter; the owner found the buyer.
why: An exclusive agency listing lets the owner sell without paying the broker.
hook: Exclusive agency: the owner keeps one exit.

q: An owner gives open listings to three brokers. Who earns a commission?
options: Only the broker who is the procuring cause of the sale
The first broker to list it
No broker, because open listings don't pay
wrong: Only the broker who produces the buyer is paid.
Listing first doesn't decide who's paid.
Open listings do pay the procuring broker.
why: With open listings, only the procuring cause of the sale is paid.
hook: Open listing: the one who brings the buyer gets paid.

q: Why are net listings illegal or discouraged in many states?
options: They create a conflict of interest between the broker and the seller over the price
They can't be placed in the MLS
wrong: Net listings can be written; that isn't the issue.
MLS rules aren't the reason they're discouraged.
Net listings don't require dual agency.
why: Because the broker keeps everything above the seller's net, the broker benefits from a sale price the seller may not understand.
hook: Net listing: the agent's gain is the seller's pain.

q: A listing expired June 1. On June 20 the owner sells directly to a buyer the broker showed the home to in May, and the listing has a 90-day protection clause. The broker is most likely:
options: Owed nothing because the listing expired
Owed nothing unless the MLS is notified
wrong: The protection clause covers buyers introduced during the listing.
The clause doesn't create a split.
MLS notice isn't the trigger.
why: A protection (safety) clause pays the broker if a buyer they introduced buys within the protection period.
hook: Introduced it? You're protected.

q: Which event terminates a listing agreement by operation of law?
wrong: Changing the price amends the listing; it doesn't end it.
A showing doesn't affect the listing.
Moving doesn't end a listing.
why: Listings are personal service contracts, so the death or incapacity of either party ends them.
hook: Personal contract: if a person goes, the listing goes.

q: A listing agreement is best described as:
options: An employment contract between the owner and the broker
A contract to sell the property to the broker
wrong: The broker is hired to market, not to buy.
A lease grants possession.
A deed transfers title.
why: A listing hires the broker to find a buyer; it's an employment contract.
hook: A listing hires the broker.

q: A salesperson takes a listing and then changes brokerages. The listing generally:
wrong: Listings are contracts with the broker, not the salesperson.
Changing firms doesn't cancel the broker's contract.
Nothing converts it to an open listing.
why: The listing contract belongs to the broker, so it stays with the brokerage.
hook: Listings belong to the broker.

q: A seller says, "Just get me $300,000 net and keep anything above that." What should the agent do?
options: Explain the conflict of interest, decline a net arrangement, and set a commission and list price the seller understands
Agree and list at the highest price the market will bear
Agree but keep the arrangement off paper
List it at $300,000 and buy it themselves
wrong: That's a net listing with a built-in conflict.
Hiding the arrangement makes the problem worse.
Buying the listing without full disclosure and the seller's informed consent is self-dealing.
why: A net listing pits the agent against the seller. Use a clear commission and a price based on market data.
hook: Net listing: the agent's gain is the seller's pain.

q: Procuring cause means the broker whose efforts started an unbroken chain of events leading to the sale.
wrong: That's the standard meaning of procuring cause.
why: True.
hook: Procuring cause started the chain.

q: A salesperson can enter into a listing agreement in their own name, separate from their broker.
wrong: Salespeople act on the broker's behalf; listings are the broker's contracts.
why: False. Listings are taken in the broker's name.
hook: Listings belong to the broker.

q: A listing can end by operation of law if the property is destroyed.
wrong: Destruction of the property, death, incapacity, and bankruptcy can end a listing by law.
why: True.
hook: No property, no listing.

q: The main purpose of a multiple listing service is to:
options: Let member brokers share listings and cooperate
wrong: Setting commissions as a group would be price fixing.
The state licenses agents.
The county records deeds.
why: An MLS is a cooperative system for sharing listing information among members.
hook: MLS: many brokers, one list.

q: Halfway through an exclusive right to sell listing, the seller fires the broker for no reason. Generally:
options: The seller can end the agency but may owe damages for breaching the contract
The seller can't end the agency under any circumstances
The broker must keep marketing the home
The listing converts to an open listing
wrong: A principal can revoke an agency, though it may be a breach.
Once the agency is revoked, the broker can't act for the seller.
Nothing converts it automatically.
why: The seller has the power to revoke the agency, but without cause they may be liable for the broker's damages.
hook: You can fire your agent; you may have to pay for it.

q: Your seller is about to sign an exclusive right to sell listing and asks what happens if their cousin buys the house. What should the agent do?
options: Explain that under this listing the commission is owed even if the cousin buys, and offer to discuss excluding the cousin in writing if appropriate
Say the cousin sale wouldn't count
Avoid the question until after they sign
Tell them to sign an open listing with the cousin
wrong: That's wrong for an exclusive right to sell.
Hiding material terms violates the agent's duty of disclosure.
Advising a separate listing with a non-broker makes no sense.
why: Explain the listing terms honestly before signing. Named exclusions must be in writing.
hook: Right to sell means the right to be paid.

q: A home listed under an exclusive right to sell at 5.5% commission sells for $510,000. What is the total commission?
hook: Price times rate equals commission.
